newsitem.title: USA: Fertilizer sales seen rising in near term-analysts.
newsitem.headline: Fertilizer sales seen rising in near term-analysts.

text.p: After a slow start, 1997 sales of fertilizer are seen increasing dramatically as soon as next week as farmers begin to make initial planting preparations, market observers said.
"It is my opinion that sales will increase as soon as next week," said John Douglas, president of Douglas Consulting in Florence, Ala.
Deals struck at an industry conference in New Orleans this week and dealers anxious to have inventory before farmers begin buying fertilizer should spur trade soon, analysts said.

"DAP (diammonium phosphate) inventories at the dealer levels are pretty minimal right now, but they are going to buy it as they need it," said Ken Johnson, author of Midwest Fertilizer Insight, a Houston, Tx-based industry newsletter.

Sales of nitrogen, phosphates and potash have been unusually slow this year because many dealers who bought early in 1996 were later burned by falling prices caused by the late planting season, analysts said.
"The buyers that were hit with falling prices last year are determined not to have that happen again this year," Douglas said.

Because the planting season started so late last year, there was a very small window after harvest where farmers could apply fertilizer, so demand waned and prices tumbled, said Bob Thwaites, futures specialist with Merrill Lynch brokerage in Winter Park, Fla.

The late harvest hit the entire industry hard. For example, on Thursday Canadian fertilizer giant Agrium, Inc said its fourth quarter earnings were adversely affected by limited applications from the weather-shortened fall season.
But some in the industry see the 1997 fertilizer shaping up normally.
"Things were pretty behind last fall but we've already started top dressing wheat in the southern part of the state, said Dan Weber, with Countrymark Cooperative based in Indianapolis, Ind.

Snowstorms and recent Arctic-like weather in Canada and North and South Dakota had slowed shipments of potash from Canada, but warmer weather should remedy that situation before demand really heats up, he said.
